fixes.explanation: Fury is it, friend. The verse says Jerusalem drank from the hand of the LORD "…the cup of His fury…" It also says she "…drained the goblet to the dregs…" That's a heavy cup, and she took it all the way down.

I get why sorrow came to mind, because a cup of sorrow sounds like a sad song on the radio. But the text names a different word: "…the cup of His fury…" Fury is the word Isaiah puts on that cup. Sorrow isn't the word he uses.
I wish that were the case, friend, but the verse says the opposite. "…among all the sons she brought up, there is no one to take her hand." Not one of them is named as stepping in to help her.

Right, and it's a hard line to read. Isaiah says, "…among all the sons she brought up, there is no one to take her hand." The same verse says, "Among all the sons she bore, there is no one to guide her." So she has no one to guide her and no one to take her hand.

That's it. "Your sons have fainted; they lie at the head of every street, like an antelope in a net." Fainted is the word the verse uses. The antelope in a net is the picture Isaiah chooses, and it sticks.

Never. The LORD says, "From that goblet, the cup of My fury, you will never drink again." That comes right after He says, "See, I have removed from your hand the cup of staggering." It's a promise with no end date and no fine print.

That's it. The LORD says, "I will place it in the hands of your tormentors…" The cup leaves Jerusalem's hand and goes to the ones who tormented her. The verse describes them as the ones who told her to lie down so they could walk over her.

Her sons are the ones lying at the head of every street back in verse 20, but they aren't who gets the cup. The LORD says, "I will place it in the hands of your tormentors…" That's who receives it. Her own sons aren't named in that verse.

The watchmen show up later in this passage, where they shout for joy. But the verse about the cup doesn't name them. Here the LORD says, "I will place it in the hands of your tormentors…" That's where the cup goes.
That's what they said: "Lie down, so we can walk over you…" It's a cruel thing to tell anyone. I think this one hurts, friend, and the LORD sees it too.
They weren't telling her to leave, baker. The tormentors said, "Lie down, so we can walk over you…" It's a hard line, and the same verse says she made her back like the ground.

Yes. The prophet says, "Put on your garments of splendor, O Jerusalem, holy city!" Right before that he tells her to clothe herself with strength. Strength and splendor, both on together, and what a change of tone after the cup of fury.
Right. The text says, "For the uncircumcised and unclean will no longer enter you." Jerusalem is called the holy city in the same verse. "No longer" is the passage's own wording.
No high price is named here. The LORD says, "You were sold for nothing, and without money you will be redeemed." It's the "without money" part that matters, baker.

Egypt. The LORD says, "At first My people went down to Egypt to live, then Assyria oppressed them without cause." He's looking back over His people's story, one place at a time. Egypt comes first, then Assyria.

It says it right there. The LORD says, "Therefore My people will know My name; therefore they will know on that day that I am He who speaks." That's what His people will know on that day. And He ends with, "Here I am!"

The verse says the opposite. "How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news…" Beautiful is the word the prophet picks. And it's the feet of the ones bringing good news that he's talking about.

Rebuilt walls would make for good news, but that's not what the messengers say to Zion. The text says they tell Zion, "Your God reigns!" That's the line they speak to her. The verse also says they proclaim peace and salvation.

Yes. Isaiah says, "For every eye will see when the LORD returns to Zion." Just before that he says, "Listen! Your watchmen lift up their voices, together they shout for joy." That return is the reason for the shouting.
Scattered would be bad news, and this verse is about joy. It says, "…the LORD has comforted His people; He has redeemed Jerusalem." The ruins are told to break forth in joy because of that.

Right. The verse says, "all the ends of the earth will see the salvation of our God." That comes after the LORD has bared His holy arm in the sight of all the nations. The ends of the earth are the ones named as seeing it.

Yes. The prophet says, "…purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the LORD." Right before that he calls out, "Depart, depart, go out from there!" He's speaking to the ones carrying the LORD's vessels, and he tells them to go out.
It's the other way around, friend. The prophet says, "For you will not leave in a hurry nor flee in haste…" So they won't leave in a hurry, and they won't flee in haste.
Right. The text says, "…you will not leave in a hurry nor flee in haste…" The reason follows right behind it: "…for the LORD goes before you…" So the answer is False.
Yes. The verse says, "…the LORD goes before you, and the God of Israel is your rear guard." He's out in front, and He's at the back too. Both ends of the line are covered.

The watchmen show up a few verses earlier, shouting for joy, but this verse doesn't name them as the rear guard. The text says, "…the LORD goes before you, and the God of Israel is your rear guard." He's the one covering the back.
